case_study_insert.main_stem: Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative (WVC) is a cooperative in the dairy processing and farming sector, owned by 64 member farms and employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2004 and led by general manager Celia Brannigan, the business supplies farmhouse cheese and butter to regional and national supermarket chains, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. WVC plans to invest $720,000 in a new cheese maturation and packing facility, financed by $300,000 member capital contributions, $280,000 retained profit and $140,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 64,000 units a year. WVC faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 7% and a skills gap has opened in cheese grading, with 14 of 38 staff not yet trained on the new grading line.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The maturation facility processed 16,200 cheese wheels last quarter, with the defect rate falling to 2.4% from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 27 to 14 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 2.8 days. Waste from trimmings and brine wash fell to 4.7% of output. A survey of 500 supermarket shoppers found that 58% would pay up to $0.60 more for eco-packaging on locally produced cheese, and 47% read origin labels before buying. A training needs analysis shows 14 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new grading line; off-the-job courses at the agricultural college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.00 to $12.66 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Dairy feed and energy input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is running at 7.2%, while consumer spending on locally produced cheese grew 4.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: WVC plans to finance part of its new cheese maturation and packing facility through $300,000 of member capital contributions rather than relying entirely on a bank loan. Explain two advantages for WVC of using member capital contributions instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Member capital contributions cost WVC nothing in interest or arrangement fees, which protects the cooperative's cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and a $140,000 bank loan commitment on the new $720,000 facility. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs, helping WVC keep its $14.00 selling price stable for supermarket contracts rather than passing increases on to shoppers who are already cautious about food-price inflation at 7.2%.

Point 2: Because WVC is a cooperative owned by 64 member farms, raising $300,000 from members deepens their financial stake and loyalty, reducing the risk that they sell milk elsewhere when prices are tight. It also preserves the democratic control of the cooperative, since no external lender can attach covenants over how the maturation facility is run or veto the hiring of the 14 untrained graders. Contributions strengthen the balance sheet without forcing members to surrender ownership, unlike a share issue by an investor-owned firm, and they signal commitment to the 4.1% growth in locally produced cheese that the members' milk depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wexford Vale Creamery Cooperative, its cooperative ownership and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: WVC is launching its locally produced farmhouse cheese range to national supermarkets. Consider a national television campaign, regional press and farmers' market sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WVC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A national TV campaign would reach millions of viewers very quickly and would build awareness of the WVC brand in the supermarket chains it supplies. However, production and airtime costs run into hundreds of thousands of dollars, and much of the audience sits outside WVC's supermarket distribution or does not buy premium locally produced cheese, so the spend would be poorly targeted for a 38-person cooperative carrying a $720,000 expansion and a $140,000 bank loan.

Regional press and farmers' market sponsorship: This is far cheaper and reaches the exact regional catchment where the 58% of surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.60 more for eco-packaging and locally produced cheese live. Sampling at farmers' markets builds trust and direct feedback at low cost. Its limitation is reach: the new national supermarket listings need national awareness, so regional press alone cannot generate the volume required to fill the maturation facility or justify the $720,000 investment.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can demonstrate the eco-packaging story to the 47% of shoppers who read origin labels, generate measurable engagement, and scale cheaply from regional to national coverage. Cost per reached shopper is low, and campaigns can be timed to supermarket launch windows. Results compound more slowly than television and depend on influencer credibility, but WVC can test messages with the 500 surveyed shoppers before committing.

Recommendation: WVC should choose social media influencer marketing, layered with small regional press adverts rather than a stand-alone buy. It is affordable, targeted at the eco-conscious segment, and nationally scalable. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a cooperative funding an expansion largely with member money; regional press and farmers' markets are rejected as the sole launch channel because its reach is regional only, insufficient for national supermarket listings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WVC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WVC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the national television campaign and regional press sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: WVC operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Explain two ways for WVC to apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to motivate its 38 employees on the maturation and grading lines.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: WVC can satisfy esteem and self-actualisation needs by giving grading-line staff responsibility for cheese quality sign-off and involving them in democratic decisions about maturation routines and shift patterns. Workers whose judgement is trusted, and who chair the quality circles that cut the defect rate from 3.6% to 2.4%, feel respected and fulfilled, which raises commitment and directly attacks the 7% absenteeism rate on the grading line.

Point 2: WVC can satisfy social needs by building team working between member-farm liaison staff and packing crews, for example celebrating member visits with shared tastings of the farmhouse cheese. Visible cooperation with the 64 member farms gives employees a sense of belonging to the cooperative's shared purpose, which is especially motivating for a members' business where profit is distributed according to each farm's milk supply. Recognising strong attendance with team rewards, rather than punishing absence, should reduce labour turnover, protect the 64,000-unit annual output and help the 14 untrained graders feel supported through the $750 agricultural college course.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid motivational application of Maslow's hierarchy identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WVC's flat democratic structure, its cooperative identity and its 7% absenteeism.

questions.question_text: WVC must improve motivation on the maturation line. Consider introducing performance-related bonus payments or a profit-sharing scheme for its 38 employees. Which should WVC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus payments: Bonuses tied to individual or team output targets give immediate, visible rewards for above-standard effort, for example hitting packing targets as the facility ramps up to serve national supermarket orders. They are simple to administer and can be targeted at the 14 untrained graders who complete the on-the-job grading certification. The drawbacks are that individual bonuses can encourage corner-cutting on quality — risking a rise from the current 2.4% defect rate — and they can create resentment between elected democratic team leaders and other staff in a cooperative that prides itself on equality among 64 member farms and 38 employees.

Profit-sharing scheme: Profit sharing distributes a share of the cooperative's surplus to all 38 employees, reinforcing the democratic, collective ethos of a member-owned business. It rewards overall performance, aligns everyone with the supermarket growth that funds the $720,000 facility, and costs nothing in lean years — the scheme simply pays less. However, payouts are annual and distant from daily effort, individual contribution is invisible, and weak individual performers free-ride on team effort, which can frustrate high performers on the grading line.

Decision: WVC should choose profit sharing, possibly with a small recognition element rather than a pure performance bonus. Profit sharing matches the cooperative identity, rewards everyone for the supermarket growth that makes the $720,000 expansion viable, and avoids the quality risks and internal divisions that individual bonuses can create — critical while absenteeism is 7% and grading skills are being rebuilt. Performance-related bonuses are rejected as the main scheme because they can undermine quality culture and equality in a member-owned flat structure, though WVC can layer spot recognition for safety and quality suggestions on top of the profit-sharing pot.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of bonus payments and profit sharing with limited application to WVC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of WVC and its cooperative structure.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of WVC with a well-justified decision explaining why performance-related bonus payments are rejected as the main scheme.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WVC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $225,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $9.50) = $225,000 ÷ $4.50 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $9.50 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WVC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. WVC's managers can compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 64,000 units to confirm the maturation facility is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 14,000 units, informing whether to ramp capacity toward the new facility before the supermarket contract volumes arrive.
2. The contribution per unit of $4.50 lets managers model any discount negotiated with supermarket chains: a 5% price cut to $13.30 would lower contribution to $3.80, so managers can check whether the extra volume still covers the $225,000 fixed costs before signing the listing agreement.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $225,000 and the margin between price and variable cost helps managers test the feasibility of the $140,000 bank loan repayments: each year the facility must contribute at least enough above break-even to service interest before any surplus is distributed to the 64 member farms.
4. Managers can use unit cost data (average total cost = $225,000 ÷ 64,000 units + $9.50 = $13.02 a unit) to benchmark quarterly performance, trace the 4.7% trimmings waste back to specific grading-line practices, and judge whether to renegotiate the $9.50 variable cost with feed and energy suppliers amid the 9.8% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $14.00 − $9.50 = $4.50, and $225,000 ÷ $4.50 = 50,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50. This is the revenue each unit of farmhouse cheese and butter contributes toward fixed costs after variable costs are covered. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, WVC's managers can set the supermarket sales budget with confidence because current output of 64,000 units clears the 50,000-unit break-even with a margin of safety of 14,000 units, so the maturation facility can absorb softer demand before losses begin. Second, the $4.50 contribution lets managers test any price negotiated with supermarket chains molecule by molecule: a $0.60 price cut would still leave $3.90 per unit, so a volume uplift above 58,000 units would keep total contribution above the $225,000 fixed costs. Third, break-even knowledge supports the $720,000 expansion appraisal: the second phase only proceeds once contracted volumes push output comfortably beyond 50,000 units, protecting the $140,000 bank loan repayment and the interests of the 64 member farms. Fourth, unit-cost analysis ($225,000 ÷ 64,000 units + $9.50 = $13.02) gives WVC a benchmark to attack the 4.7% trimmings waste, identify whether the $9.50 variable cost should be renegotiated against the 9.8% input-cost inflation, and decide whether to keep grading in-house or outsource during the 14-person skills gap.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WVC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has WVC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.66 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.91 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $160,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $325,000; 2025 current assets = $145,000 + $155,000 + $50,000 = $350,000. 2024 = $325,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.30; 2025 = $350,000 ÷ $225,000 = 1.56. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($325,000 − $160,000) ÷ $250,000 = $165,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.66; 2025 = ($350,000 − $145,000) ÷ $225,000 = $205,000 ÷ $225,000 = 0.91.

Evaluation: WVC's liquidity has strengthened. The improvement in coverage of short-term obligations is helped by current liabilities falling from $250,000 to $225,000 while current assets rose from $325,000 to $350,000, partly reflecting the $50,000 cash build-up as supermarket contracts converted to receivables. The acid test, which strips out inventories of cheese wheels in maturation, moved from 0.66 to 0.91, so WVC now almost covers short-term debts without selling stock — essential while it services the $140,000 bank loan and stages the $720,000 facility. However, trade receivables rose from $130,000 to $155,000, meaning more cash is tied up with supermarket customers; if they stretch payment terms, the stronger position could deteriorate. Inventories fell from $160,000 to $145,000, so stock availability for peak Christmas cheese demand should be monitored rather than assumed.

Conclusion: WVC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures show clearer coverage of current liabilities, and the improvement does not rely on inventories, which actually fell. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so WVC should tighten supermarket credit terms and monitor collection while proceeding with the facility build-out and continuing to serve its 64 member farms.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether WVC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WVC of introducing paper-based eco-packaging for its farmhouse cheese range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Paper-based eco-packaging matches the values of the 58% of shoppers in WVC's market research who would pay up to $0.60 more for such packaging, allowing WVC to hold or raise its $14.00 selling price and protect its $4.50 contribution per unit while input costs rise 9.8%. It also appeals to the 47% of shoppers who read origin labels, strengthening the local, member-farm story that wins national supermarket listings for the new $720,000 maturation facility and supporting the 4.1% growth in locally produced cheese spending.

Disadvantage: Sustainable paper and coatings typically cost more than conventional plastic or wax wrap, raising the $9.50 variable cost per unit and squeezing the contribution margin unless the $0.60 premium is accepted across the whole range. Paper can also offer a shorter shelf life or weaker moisture barrier for maturing cheese; any rise in damage or mould would push the current 2.4% defect rate upward and increase trimmings waste above 4.7%, eroding the gains the new facility is meant to deliver — especially before the 14 untrained graders complete their on-the-job certification.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WVC's research data, cost structure, quality figures and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs will affect WVC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): With a $140,000 bank loan attached to the $720,000 facility, if WVC's loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 0.75%, adding roughly $1,050 a year to financing costs — real but modest against fixed costs of $225,000. Higher rates also cool consumer appetite for premium locally produced cheese and raise the cost of any future borrowing to complete the facility. The direct cash impact is the smallest of the three changes and can be partly managed by fixing the loan rate or accelerating member contributions.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.66 per hour from April 2026): WVC's workforce of 38, weighted toward grading, maturation and packing, faces a materially higher wage bill. If average hourly pay moves from about $12.00 to $12.66, the annual cost of one full-time employee rises by roughly $1,400, adding perhaps $53,000 a year across 38 staff — a significant burden for a cooperative whose member farms also face rising feed costs, though higher productivity on the new grading line (64,000 units ÷ 38 employees ≈ 1,684 units per worker) can offset part of it.

Input cost inflation (9.8% dairy feed and energy): WVC's $9.50 variable cost is dominated by milk, feed and energy. A 9.8% rise on even the feed-and-energy component adds roughly $0.55–$0.93 per unit; at 64,000 units that is about $35,000–$60,000 a year, cutting contribution from $4.50 toward $3.60–$3.95 and undermining the margin that justifies the maturation facility — though WVC can recover part through the $0.60 eco-packaging premium and supermarket price negotiations.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in dairy feed and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. It compresses the $4.50 contribution on every one of the 64,000 units WVC sells and feeds straight into member farmers' own costs, threatening the whole cooperative model. The wage rise is the second most serious pressure, while the interest rate increase is the smallest in cash terms and can be managed by fixing rates — but WVC must act on all three, prioritising input-cost control, premium pricing and productivity gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to WVC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WVC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of WVC with a well-justified judgement that the 9.8% input-cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
